verses.zh: 众子啊，要听父亲的教训，留心得知聪明。
verses.en: Listen, children,[NOTE:1] to a father’s instruction,[NOTE:2] and pay attention so that you may gain[NOTE:3] discernment.
notes: The chapter includes an exhortation to acquire wisdom (1-4a), a list of the benefits of wisdom (4b-9), a call to pursue a righteous lifestyle (10-13), a warning against a wicked lifestyle (14-19), and an exhortation to righteousness (20-27).
Heb “sons.” See note at 1:8.
Or “warning.” See note at 1:2.

verses.zh: 因我所给你们的是好教训；不可离弃我的法则（或译：指教）。
verses.en: Because I hereby give[NOTE:1] you good instruction,do not forsake my teaching.
notes: Heb “in order to come to know.” As a stative verb, יָדַע (yadaʿ) can mean “to know” or “to come to know,” the latter essentially meaning “to learn.” The infinitive indicates the purpose of the earlier imperatives.

verses.zh: 我在父亲面前为孝子，在母亲眼中为独一的娇儿。
verses.en: When I was a son to my father,[NOTE:1] a tender, only child[NOTE:2] before my mother,
notes: The perfect tense has the nuance of instantaneous (or performative) perfect; the sage is now calling the disciples to listen. It could also be a perfect of resolve, indicating what he is determined to do, or a present perfect reflecting his proven past history, “Indeed I have given you X.”
Or “a boy with my father.”

verses.zh: 父亲教训我说：你心要存记我的言语，遵守我的命令，便得存活。
verses.en: he taught me, and he said to me:“Let your heart lay hold of my words;keep my commands so that[NOTE:1] you will live.
notes: Heb “tender and only one.” The phrase רַךְ וְיָחִיד (rakh veyakhid, “tender and only one”) is a hendiadys meaning “tender only child.” The adjective רַךְ (rakh) means “tender; delicate” (BDB 940 s.v. רַךְ), and describes a lad who is young and undeveloped in character (e.g., 2 Sam 3:39). The adjective יָחִיד (yakhid) means “only one” (BDB 402 s.v. יָחִיד) and refers to a beloved and prized only child (e.g., Gen 22:2). tc The LXX introduces the ideas of “obedient” and “beloved” for these two terms. This seems to be a free rendering, if not a translation of a different Hebrew textual tradition. The MT makes good sense and requires no emendation.

verses.zh: 要得智慧，要得聪明，不可忘记，也不可偏离我口中的言语。
verses.en: Acquire wisdom, acquire understanding;do not forget and do not turn aside from the words I speak.[NOTE:1]
notes: The vav plus imperative “and live” expresses purpose, as is common with volitional verbs in a series.

verses.zh: 不可离弃智慧，智慧就护卫你；要爱她，她就保守你。
verses.en: Do not forsake wisdom,[NOTE:1] and she will protect you;love her, and she will guard you.
notes: Heb “from the words of my mouth” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV); TEV, CEV “what I say.”sn The verse repeats the imperative “acquire” to underscore the importance of getting wisdom.

verses.zh: 智慧为首；所以，要得智慧。在你一切所得之内必得聪明（或译：用你一切所得的去换聪明）。
verses.en: Wisdom is supreme[NOTE:1]—so[NOTE:2] acquire wisdom,and whatever you acquire,[NOTE:3] acquire understanding![NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “her.” The referent of the pronoun is personified “wisdom,” which has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The absolute and construct state of רֵאשִׁית (reʾshit) are identical (BDB 912 s.v.). Some treat רֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה (reʾshit khokhmah) as a genitive-construct phrase: “the beginning of wisdom” (cf. NAB, NASB, NRSV). Others take רֵאשִׁית as an absolute functioning as predicate and חָכְמָה as the subject: “wisdom is the first/chief thing” (cf. KJV, ASV). The context here suggests the predicate.
The term “so” does not appear in the Hebrew but is supplied in the translation for the sake of smoothness and style.

The noun קִנְיָן (qinyan) means “thing got or acquired; acquisition” (BDB 889 s.v.). With the preposition that denotes price, it means “with (or at the price of) all that you have acquired.” The point is that no price is too high for wisdom—give everything for it (K&D 16:108).

verses.zh: 高举智慧，她就使你高升；怀抱智慧，她就使你尊荣。
verses.en: Esteem her highly[NOTE:1] and she will exalt you;she will honor you if you embrace her.
notes: The verse is not in the LXX; some textual critics delete the verse as an impossible gloss that interrupts vv. 6 and 8 (e.g., C. H. Toy, Proverbs [ICC], 88).

verses.zh: 她必将华冠加在你头上，把荣冕交给你。
verses.en: She will place a fair[NOTE:1] garland on your head;she will bestow a beautiful crown[NOTE:2] on you.”
notes: The verb is the Pilpel imperative from סָלַל (salal). In its ten Qal uses, it means to pile up, usually in building a road. The two uses in the doubling stems (here and Exod 9:17) are resultative or plurative, meaning “to raise up, to exalt.” To grant her a high position implies esteeming her.
The personification of wisdom continues with the bestowal of a wreath for the head (e.g., 1:9). The point is that grace will be given to the individual like a wreath about the head.

verses.zh: 我儿，你要听受我的言语，就必延年益寿。
verses.en: Listen, my child,[NOTE:1] and accept my wordsso that[NOTE:2] the years of your life will be many.[NOTE:3]
notes: This verse uses wedding imagery: The wife (wisdom) who is embraced by her husband (the disciple) will place the wedding crown on the head of her new bridegroom. Wisdom, like a virtuous wife, will crown the individual with honor and grace. In vv. 4-9 Murphy points out the four fold repetition of “acquire” (קָנָה, qanah), the same term used of Boaz taking Ruth as a wife (Ruth 4:8, 10), and the calls to love her (Prov 4:6) and embrace her (4:8) (R. Murphy, Proverbs [WBC], 27). This section personifies wisdom and portrays the pursuit of wisdom as a paramount romantic pursuit.
Heb “my son” (likewise in v. 20).
Following an imperative, a vav plus imperfect verb can depict purpose or result.

verses.zh: 我已指教你走智慧的道，引导你行正直的路。
verses.en: I hereby guide you[NOTE:1] in the way of wisdom,and I lead you in upright paths.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and the years of life will be many for you.”

The verb יָרָה (yarah) means “to teach; to instruct; to guide.” This is from the same root as the Hebrew word for “law” (torah). See G. R. Driver, “Hebrew Notes,” VT 1 (1951): 241-50; and J. L. Crenshaw, “The Acquisition of Knowledge in Israelite Wisdom Literature,” WW 7 (1986): 9.tn The form הֹרֵתִיךָ (horetikha) is the Hiphil perfect with a suffix from the root יָרָה (yarah, “to guide”). This and the parallel verb should be taken as instantaneous (or performative) perfects, translated as an English present tense: The sage is now instructing or pointing the way.

verses.zh: 你行走，脚步必不致狭窄；你奔跑，也不致跌倒。
verses.en: When you walk, your steps[NOTE:1] will not be hampered,[NOTE:2] and when you run,[NOTE:3] you will not stumble.
notes: Heb “in the tracks of uprightness”; cf. NAB “on straightforward paths.” Both the verb and the object of the preposition make use of the idiom—the verb is the Hiphil perfect from דֶּרֶךְ (derekh, related to “road; way”) and the object is “wagon tracks, paths.”

The noun צַעֲדֶךָ (tsaʿadekha, “your steps”) and the temporal infinitive בְּלֶכְתְּךָ (belekhtekha, “when you walk”) use the idiom of walking to represent the course of life. On that course there will be no obstacles; the “path” will be straight—morally and practically.

The verb צָרַר (tsarar, “to be narrow; to be constricted”) refers to that which is narrow or constricted, signifying distress, trouble, adversity; that which was wide-open or broad represents freedom and deliverance.

verses.zh: 要持定训诲，不可放松；必当谨守，因为它是你的生命。
verses.en: Hold on to instruction,[NOTE:1] do not let it go;protect it,[NOTE:2] because it is your life.
notes: The progression from walking to running is an idiom called “anabasis,” suggesting that as greater and swifter progress is made, there will be nothing to impede the progress (e.g., Isa 40:31).
Or “discipline.” See note at 1:2.

verses.zh: 不可行恶人的路；不要走坏人的道。
verses.en: Do not enter the path of the wickedor walk[NOTE:1] in the way of those who are evil.
notes: The form נִצְּרֶהָ (nitsereha, from נָצַר, natsar) has an anomalous doubled letter (see GKC 73 §20.h).

verses.zh: 要躲避，不可经过；要转身而去。
verses.en: Avoid it, do not go on it;turn away from it, and go on.[NOTE:1]
notes: The verb אָשַׁר (ʾashar, “to walk”) is not to be confused with the identically spelled homonym אָשַׁר “to pronounce happy” as in BDB 80 s.v. אָשַׁר.

verses.zh: 这等人若不行恶，不得睡觉；不使人跌倒，睡卧不安；
verses.en: For they cannot sleep[NOTE:1] unless they cause harm;[NOTE:2] they are robbed of sleep[NOTE:3] until they make someone stumble.[NOTE:4]
notes: The verb עָבַר (ʿavar, “to cross over; to travel through”) ends both cola. In the first it warns against going on wrong paths; in the second it means “to go your own way,” but may hint that the way will cross over the wrong way. The rapid sequence of commands stresses the urgency of the matter.
The verb יָשֵׁן (yashen) “to be asleep” is a stative root. In the imperfect it can be future “will not sleep” or modal, in this case abilitive, “are not able to sleep.”

The verb is רָעַע (raʿaʿ), which means “to do evil; to harm.” The verse is using the figure of hyperbole to stress the preoccupation of some people with causing trouble. R. L. Alden says, “How sick to find peace only at the price of another man’s misfortune” (Proverbs, 47).
Heb “their sleep is robbed/seized”; these expressions are metonymical for their restlessness in plotting evil.

verses.zh: 因为他们以奸恶吃饼，以强暴喝酒。
verses.en: Indeed they have eaten[NOTE:1] bread gained from wickedness[NOTE:2] and drink[NOTE:3] wine obtained from violence.[NOTE:4]
notes: The Hiphil imperfect (Kethib) means “cause to stumble.” This idiom (from hypocatastasis) means “bring injury/ruin to someone” (BDB 505-6 s.v. כָּשַׁל Hiph.1).
The verb ‏לָחֲמוּ (lakhamu) is a perfect form of a dynamic root, and therefore past or perfective. This serves as verification of the description in the previous verse.

Heb “the bread of wickedness” (so KJV, NAB, NIV, NRSV). There are two ways to take the genitives: (1) genitives of apposition: wickedness and violence are their food and drink (cf. TEV, CEV, NLT), or (2) genitives of source: they derive their livelihood from the evil they do (C. H. Toy, Proverbs [ICC], 93).

The verb is an imperfect, either present or future, saying what they do or forecasting what they will do. Being paired with a perfect verb in the beginning of the verse, the description combines their past pattern with what they continue to do.

verses.zh: 但义人的路好像黎明的光，越照越明，直到日午。
verses.en: But the path of the righteous is like the bright morning light,[NOTE:1] growing brighter and brighter[NOTE:2] until full day.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “the wine of violence” (so KJV, NAB, NIV, NRSV). This is a genitive of source, meaning that the wine they drink was plundered from their violent crime. The Hebrew is structured in an AB:BA chiasm: “For they eat the bread of wickedness, and the wine of violence they drink.” The word order in the translation is reversed for the sake of smoothness and readability.

Heb “like light of brightness.” This construction is an attributive genitive: “bright light.” The word “light” (אוֹר, ʾor) refers to the early morning light or the dawn (BDB 21 s.v.). The point of the simile is that the course of life that the righteous follow is like the clear, bright morning light. It is illumined, clear, easy to follow, and healthy and safe—the opposite of what darkness represents.

A literal rendering would appear to be “walking and becoming bright.” When the Qal active participle of הָלַךְ (halakh) is paired with another participle (or adj.) it can express the intensification of an event, that is, the second element in the pairing continues on and increases in character. Cf. Jonah 1:11 and see HALOT 246-247 s.v. הָלַךְ 5).

verses.zh: 恶人的道好像幽暗，自己不知因甚么跌倒。
verses.en: The way of the wicked is like gloomy darkness;they do not know what they stumble over.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “until the day is established.” This expression refers to the coming of the full day or the time of high noon.

verses.zh: 我儿，要留心听我的言词，侧耳听我的话语，
verses.en: My child, pay attention to my words;listen attentively[NOTE:1] to my sayings.
notes: The image of paths, brightness or darkness, and stumbling illustrate the contrast of lifestyles. When acting with righteousness one’s course becomes clearer and more sure, while the wicked are caught in their ways, ignorant of why they fall.

verses.zh: 都不可离你的眼目，要存记在你心中。
verses.en: Do not let them depart[NOTE:1] from your sight;guard[NOTE:2] them within your heart,[NOTE:3]
notes: Commentators note the use of the body in this section: ear (v. 20), eyes (v. 21), flesh (v. 22), heart (v. 23), lips (v. 24), eyes (v. 25), feet (v. 26), and hands and feet (v. 27). Each is a synecdoche of part representing the whole; the total accumulation signifies the complete person in the process.tn Heb “incline your ear.” The verb הַט (hat) is the Hiphil imperative from נָטָה (natah, Hiphil: “to turn to; to incline”). The idiom “to incline the ear” gives the picture of “lean over and listen closely.”
The Hiphil form יַלִּיזוּ (yallizu) follows the Aramaic with gemination. The verb means “to turn aside; to depart” (intransitive Hiphil or inner causative).
Or “keep” (so KJV, NIV, NRSV and many others).

verses.zh: 因为得着它的，就得了生命，又得了医全体的良药。
verses.en: for they are life to those who find them and healing to one’s entire body.[NOTE:1]
notes: The words “eyes” and “heart” are metonymies of subject representing the faculties of each. Cf. CEV “think about it all.”

verses.zh: 你要保守你心，胜过保守一切（或译：你要切切保守你心），因为一生的果效是由心发出。
verses.en: Guard your heart[NOTE:1] with all vigilance,[NOTE:2] for from it are the sources[NOTE:3] of life.
notes: Heb “to all of his flesh.”

Anatomically the Hebrew word לֵב (lev) refers to the “heart.” But abstractly it can refer to one’s inner self, will, understanding, or mind. They did not see the heart and mind in opposition, such that the advice here includes both one’s thinking and feelings.

Heb “more than any guard.” The preposition מִן (min) has its comparative sense “more than.” The noun מִשְׁמָר (mishmar) refers here to the act of guarding, protection, or vigilance (BDB 1038 s.v. מִשְׁמָר; HALOT 649 s.v. מִשְׁמָר).

verses.zh: 你要除掉邪僻的口，弃绝乖谬的嘴。
verses.en: Remove perverse speech[NOTE:1] from your mouth;[NOTE:2] keep devious talk far from your lips.[NOTE:3]
notes: The word תּוֹצְאוֹת (totseʾot, from יָצָא, yatsaʾ) means “outgoings; extremities; sources.” It is used here for starting points, like a fountainhead, and so the translation “sources” works well.

Heb “crookedness.” The noun עִקְּשׁוּת (ʿiqqeshut) refers to what is morally twisted or perverted. Here it refers to things that are said (cf. NAB “dishonest talk”; NRSV “crooked speech”). The term “mouth” functions as a metonymy of cause for perverse speech. Such perverse talking could be subtle or blatant.
Heb “crookedness of mouth.”

verses.zh: 你的眼目要向前正看；你的眼睛（原文是皮）当向前直观。
verses.en: Let your eyes look directly[NOTE:1] in front of you,and let your gaze[NOTE:2] look straight before you.
notes: Heb “deviousness of lips put far from you.”
The jussives in this verse are both Hiphil, the first from the verb “to gaze; to look intently [or, carefully],” (נָבַט, navat) and the second from the verb “to be smooth, straight” (יָשָׁר, yashar).

verses.zh: 要修平你脚下的路，坚定你一切的道。
verses.en: Make the path for your feet[NOTE:1] level,[NOTE:2] so that[NOTE:3] all your ways may be established.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “your eyelids.” The term “eyelids” is often a poetic synonym for “eye” (it is a metonymy of adjunct, something connected with the eye put for the eye that sees); it may intensify the idea as one might squint to gain a clearer look.
Heb “path of your foot.”

The verb is a denominative Piel from the word פֶּלֶס (peles), “balance; scale.” In addition to telling the disciple to keep focused on a righteous life, the sage tells him to keep his path level, which is figurative for living the righteous life.
Following an imperative, a vav plus imperfect verb can depict purpose or result.

verses.zh: 不可偏向左右；要使你的脚离开邪恶。
verses.en: Do not turn[NOTE:1] to the right or to the left;turn yourself[NOTE:2] away from evil.[NOTE:3]
notes: The Niphal jussive from כּוּן (kun, “to be fixed; to be established; to be steadfast”) continues the idiom of walking and ways for the moral sense in life.

The two verbs in this verse are from different roots, but nonetheless share the same semantic domain. The first verb is תֵּט (tet), a jussive from נָטָה (natah), which means “to turn aside” (Hiphil); the second verb is the Hiphil imperative of סוּר (sur), which means “to cause to turn to the side” (Hiphil). The disciple is not to leave the path of righteousness, but to stay on the path he must leave evil.
Heb “your foot” (so NAB, NIV, NRSV). The term רַגְלְךָ (raglekha, “your foot”) is a synecdoche of part (= foot) for the whole person (= “yourself”).
